signals.source_text: Story points are becoming outdated for AI-driven development. When your team is made of AI agents, I think we need a different way to understand the work. Instead of asking only: “How many story points did we complete?” I want to see: → how many tokens were spent → how much machine time was used → what actually progressed → where agents are blocked → how much work is waiting for a human That is why I built a local Kanban into my Claude Code telemetry dashboard. I use it as a real-time operational view of my AI team. The Kanban itself is deliberately simple: BACKLOG → IN PROGRESS → BLOCKED → REVIEW → DONE Each task is connected to the existing telemetry, so I can see the agent, project, branch, duration, tokens, output, weighted usage and machine time without duplicating the data. But the real value for me is not the Kanban itself. It is the combination of two very different information layers. Confluence is the knowledge and decision layer. That is where I keep: → project goals and context → questions that require my input → decisions and decision tracking → results and findings → documentation produced by the agents Agents periodically write there, and I work with that information asynchronously. The dashboard is the operational layer. It gives me a real-time picture of what the AI team is doing right now: → which tasks are running → which agents are working → what is blocked → what is waiting for review → how much machine time and tokens are being consumed So I don’t need to constantly jump between Claude sessions to understand what is happening. I can work asynchronously through Confluence while keeping the real-time operational picture in the dashboard. And this is where I find the combination particularly useful. For example, a task might have been “IN PROGRESS” for three hours, but the actual machine time could be only 40 minutes. That shows me that the remaining time was spent waiting, for another agent, a dependency, or me. The key when working with an AI team is to pay close attention not just to agent activity, but to how efficiently the team produces a real, deliverable outcome. For example: • for customer pipeline optimization - the number and quality of ready-to-send recommendations that can be directly shared with the customer; • for an AI bug-fixer - the number of successfully fixed bugs relative to the number of tokens consumed; • for any other workflow - define a specific, measurable outcome and evaluate it against the AI resources consumed.
